critic:factcheck.summary: Of about 33 sourced claim groups checked against their primary pages through Exa, 31 are supported as written, and none of the inputs that drive the recommendation, the cost model or the ranking is contradicted; the report's sourcing is unusually sound. findings.section: Section 10 Federal row and the FDA discussion
findings.quoted_text: FDA: dental laboratories making devices to a licensed practitioner's prescription are exempt from establishment registration and listing under 21 CFR 807.65(i)
findings.problem: The paraphrase is broader than the regulation. 807.65(i) exempts persons "whose major responsibility is to render a service necessary to provide the consumer ... with a device", listing "dental laboratory" among establishments "whose primary responsibility to the ultimate consumer is to dispense or provide a service through the use of a previously manufactured device." The text does not say labs "making devices to prescription" are exempt; the service-on-a-previously-manufactured-device framing is precisely why milling implant-connecting geometry is the open question the report raises. The citation itself could not be opened at eCFR (bot block) and was verified via Cornell LII.
findings.evidence: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/807.65 (eCFR returned a CAPTCHA request): "(i) Persons who dispense devices to the ultimate consumer or whose major responsibility is to render a service necessary to provide the consumer (i.e., patient, physician, layman, etc.) with a device or the benefits to be derived from the use of a device; for example, a hearing aid dispenser, optician, clinical laboratory, assembler of diagnostic x-ray systems, and personnel from a hospital, clinic, dental laboratory, orthotic or prosthetic retail facility, whose primary responsibility to the ultimate consumer is to dispense or provide a service through the use of a previously manufactured device."
findings.suggested_fix: Reword to: "FDA: 21 CFR 807.65(i) exempts dental laboratories whose primary responsibility is to provide a service to the dentist through the use of a previously manufactured device (the traditional prescription-lab exemption); it does not on its face cover a lab that manufactures an implant-connecting component on its own parameters, which is the clearance question below." Cite https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/807.65 as the readable copy.

critic:skeptic.summary: The report's regulatory and price facts hold up: I re-read the FDA FY2027 fee notice ($13,785), RCW 70.352.050, the Oregon HLO permanent rule (out-of-state scope, $250 + $500 fees, Oct 31 waiver), Glidewell's live prices, the Hawaii Data Book (Maui 116 dentists), the GoldStreak chart, Rev. Proc. 2025-32 and the WSDA PNDC dates, and all match. The recommendation itself is much weaker than the prose suggests. Option A's base case is negative after owner time (-$143), it ranks first only because of analyst judgment scores (on the four quantitative criteria alone it sits sixth, behind B, J, D, K and L), and its demand evidence is no better than the distant markets': the report's own Puget Sound research agent wrote "there is no evidence it is underserved... claims of unmet need would be speculation," which the report never discloses, while using absolute lab counts to call Orange County structurally hopeless even though Washington and California have essentially identical labs-per-dentist ratios (1 per 40 vs 1 per 41). The conversion funnel in Section 12.1 does not compute (10 trial cases at the stated 15-25% trial-to-recurring rate yields 1.5-2.5 accounts, not 3-6), half of A's modeled revenue comes from $129 commodity crowns the report says cannot be sold against Glidewell/Dandy, and the model charges 30 founder hours a month while the plan schedules about 59. The same 90-day program is budgeted at $9,700, $5,650 (table sums to $5,290), $4,750, $4,200 and $5,000 in different sections. Against the brief, the report only nominally compares operating models per geography (only South OC gets all six), details a "top three" that is not the ranking's top three, runs four streams inside the 90 days despite the "one complementary initiative" rule, uses two stress tests that are vacuous or misdescribed, cites a non-existent Appendix B for switching evidence, and relies on a 2019 FedEx guide and an unquoted Pirate Ship discount for the Maui lane. The "grow in place, no lease" conclusion is probably still right, but mainly because every alternative is worse, not because A's case is proven; the report should say so and fix the arithmetic that currently flatters A.

findings.quoted_text: Thirty conversations in eight weeks, ten trial cases accepted, three to six recurring accounts by month 6 to 9 (15 to 25 percent on warm introductions
findings.problem: The funnel arithmetic contradicts the report's own stated rate. Section 6 defines the 15-25 percent as a trial-to-recurring conversion. Ten trials at 15-25 percent yields 1.5 to 2.5 recurring accounts, not 3 to 6. Reaching the base case of 6 accounts at that rate requires 24-40 trial cases, which is 80-130 percent of the 30 conversations converting to a trial. Gate 3 (4 recurring from 15 cumulative trials) implies 27 percent, above the top of the range. Either the rate is conversation-to-recurring (then 10 trials to 3-6 accounts is 30-60 percent trial conversion, unsupported) or the base case is unreachable on the report's own assumptions.
findings.evidence: report.md Section 6: 'Expect a 15 to 25 percent trial-to-recurring conversion on warm introductions'; Section 12.1 funnel; Section 14 week 11 'Cumulative trial cases 15 or more; recurring accounts 4 or more'; model/inputs.json bellevue_grow accounts_12m [3,6,10]. 10 x 0.15-0.25 = 1.5-2.5; 6 / 0.25 = 24 trials, 6 / 0.15 = 40 trials.
findings.suggested_fix: Restate the funnel consistently: e.g., 40 conversations -> 20-24 trial cases -> 3-6 recurring accounts (15-25 percent trial-to-recurring), and raise the week-4/8 gate targets for trials accordingly (at least 8 trials by gate 1, 16 by gate 2), or lower the base case to 3-4 accounts and re-run the model and ranking.

findings.section: 11 Ranking and sensitivity; 12.1 Why it ranks first
findings.quoted_text: Highest fit and evidence scores. Positive after owner time at base, strongly positive at high, and the only option that reduces the Jung concentration.
findings.problem: Two problems. (1) 'Positive after owner time at base' is false: Section 8.3 and outputs.md show A's base year-1 profit after owner time is -$143 and the report itself calls it 'breakeven'. (2) A ranks first only because of the analyst judgment scores (fit 5, evidence 4, speed 4 = 13 points, the highest of any option; B has 10). On the four model-derived criteria alone (profit, cash, time efficiency, downside) A scores 2.86, below K/L 3.29, B 3.21, J 3.14 and D 3.00. The 30 percent of weight assigned to judgment is what produces the answer, and the profit banding is fragile: M at +$232 scores 3 while A at -$143 scores 2, a $375 gap worth a full point.
findings.evidence: model/ranking.py bands and J dict; model/ranking.md row 1 (A profit 2, cash 3, time 4, downside 3, fit 5, evidence 4, speed 4; base yr-1 profit -$143). Recomputed quant-only scores with the balanced weights (25/20/15/10 over 70): A 2.86, B 3.21, J 3.14, D 3.00, K/L 3.29, M 2.71.
findings.suggested_fix: Change 12.1 to 'Breakeven (-$143) after owner time at base'. In Section 11 add a sentence: 'On the four quantitative criteria alone A ranks sixth; it leads only after fit, evidence and speed are added, which are my judgments.' Show a quant-only column in the ranking table and justify the evidence score of 4 or lower it to 3.

findings.section: 1 The direct recommendation, point 3; 4.1 Puget Sound baseline
findings.quoted_text: The Puget Sound market you are standing in is the richest one on the list for your specific capabilities.
findings.problem: The demand case for growing in place is asserted, not evidenced, and is no better supported than the distant markets. The report's own Puget Sound research agent concluded the market is 'already served by roughly 30 named independent labs in King County alone... There is no evidence it is underserved' and listed 'Any evidence of dentist dissatisfaction with existing local labs: none was found; claims of unmet need would be speculation.' None of this appears in the report. The 'structural problem' used to disqualify Orange County (most lab-dense state) rests on absolute counts: per dentist, Washington (175 labs / 7,071 dentists, 1 per 40) and California (734 / 30,280, 1 per 41) are identical. Dentist density per 100,000 is not a measure of available outsourced lab demand. The only local 'evidence' is Dr. Kim (trial not yet converted; Draft 7 still asks for the second case) and Harmony Dental, an inbound remote account acquired through Medit Link, which supports the scanner-network channel rather than drop-offs.
findings.evidence: research/puget_market.json summary and unknowns (quoted above); research/soc_market.json unknowns: 'Any public complaints or documented dissatisfaction by south-OC dentists with local labs: none found; do not assume it.'; report.md 4.1 and 4.2 figures 175 WA labs, 734 CA labs, 7,071 WA dentists, 30,280 CA dentists; outreach/drafts.md Draft 7.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the agent's caveat verbatim to Sections 1 and 4.1, replace 'richest one on the list' with 'the only market where you already have relationships, no shipping cost and no new nexus', present labs-per-dentist for WA vs CA, and lower A's evidence score to 3 (same as the remote options) unless real local conversion data exists.

findings.quoted_text: for option A the base mix per account is 6 zirconia crowns, 1.5 implant crowns, 0.15 full arches and 0.8 night guards a month
findings.problem: The model and the strategy contradict each other. Section 12.1 says the offer is implant crowns and full arches and 'Nothing else is offered in the first meeting'; Section 4.1 and Table 5 say you 'cannot win on price' and cannot win 'Commodity posterior crowns at $129 against $89 to $99 national offers'. Yet 51 percent of A's modeled revenue per account ($774 of $1,526) and about half its contribution comes from exactly those $129 crowns (6 per account per month). Full arches, the headline product, are 0.15 per account per month (about 11 arches a year across 6 accounts). If the crowns had to be priced at Glidewell's $109 to win them, contribution falls roughly $116 per account per month and A's base year-1 result drops from -$143 to about -$6,100.
findings.evidence: model/inputs.json bellevue_grow case_mix and products.fcz_crown price [99,129,129]; report.md 8.2 ($129 crown $70 base contribution), 12.1 ('Nothing else is offered in the first meeting'), Table 5 row 1. Arithmetic: 6 x $129 = $774 / $1,526 = 50.7 percent; 51 account-months x 6 crowns x $19.40 = about $5,900.
findings.suggested_fix: Either re-weight the base mix toward the products the offer actually sells (e.g., 2 crowns, 2 implant crowns, 0.3 arches) and re-run, or add a stress row 'crown price matched to $109' and state plainly that the base case depends on winning commodity crowns at $129 from practices that can get them for $89-$109 with free shipping.

findings.section: 13 What to run; 14 The 90-day plan; 16 What I would do; 7.4

critic:model.summary: The model's arithmetic is sound: running model.py and ranking.py in a scratch copy reproduces outputs.md and ranking.md byte for byte, and four hand recomputations match exactly (option A base monthly cash $1,440; option E base first 90 days $13,099.5 → $13,100; option C base year-1 profit after owner time −$22,850; zirconia crown on the Hawaii lane $20.36 → $20). Every number in the report's tables in Sections 7.1, 8.3, 8.4 and 11 matches outputs.md and ranking.md, as do the itemized stacks in 7.2 and the pairwise comparisons in 8.6. The problems are in definitions, assumptions and narrative rather than in the formulas. Logic issues: option A charges King County delivery twice (a $300/month "mileage and courier" line plus $10 per case inside contribution, about $332/month at six accounts), which alone moves A's base-case year-1 profit from −$143 to +$3,457 and its profit band from 2 to 3; the "remake rate doubles" stress is a flat 5%-of-revenue haircut (2.6x the true effect) and Section 8.1 misdescribes remakes as a percent of price; maximum drawdown ignores the pre-revenue startup outlay (M high shows a positive "drawdown"); lease options count the prepaid rent month twice; option I's exit exposure omits the pass-through the stated definition includes. Assumption issues: the Hawaii lane ($55/$95/$150) contradicts the report's own cited FedEx One Rate table, where 2Day small box to Hawaii is $19.55 each way (and USPS Priority Mail small flat-rate is $12.95–14.65), so the headline "$20 crown" would be about $53 and H's contribution per account about $529 rather than $320 (the Maui verdict still holds); the model charges all technician labor at $40/hour as variable while the capacity note assumes 290–360 hours of already-paid staff time (payroll of $3,360/month buys 84 hours at that rate); founder hours are 30/month in the model but about 59/month in the 90-day plan; receivables lag and the dealer's machine-purchase float are set to zero although the report names both as risks. Narrative mismatches: Section 11 says the South OC remote option is "fifth" and the office "tenth" under the lifestyle weighting when ranking.md has D tied for first (3.70) and E eighth; Section 12 calls B "third" and treats C as a top-three option while Section 11 ranks B second, J third and C ninth; the Section 14 budget table sums to $5,290, not $5,650, and three different 90-day figures are given for the $5,000 envelope ($4,200, $4,750, about $2,750 plus reserve); gate 3 demands four recurring accounts by month 3 when the base-case ramp delivers 2.25; "A plus C near $17,000 collected" adds cash flows to revenue (revenue would be about $23,800). The ranking is transparent and A and B remain the top two under every weighting and under five alternative constructions I tested, but A's 0.05 edge over B rests entirely on analyst judgment (A beats B only on fit/evidence/speed; one point less on A's evidence score puts B first), third place (J) is a cheapness artifact of using exit exposure as "downside," and C ties A for first (3.35) rather than "sits second" when the FDA fee is removed. Fixing the courier double count makes A's lead robust (3.60 vs 3.30), so the recommendation survives review, but the report should correct the mismatches and state the hour and lane assumptions it actually relies on.
